title: Hypermaterialism
content:
is an artist based in New York.

Do Not Research is a reader-supported publication:

Introduction

It feels like in the last couple years there have been a lot of glossy PR pieces telling us that the names we loved during the gritty early days of Web 2 are making a resurgence, that Post-Net is back on the cutting edge. In a real sense, the stars of Post-Net are back. The most interesting work in most biennials and museum shows can still often be determined by whether the artists behind it had anything to do with the DIS Berlinale. Brad Troemel and Josh Citarella are both separately influencers that have broken through to total normies; Avery Singer seems to be gearing up a press cycle for a 3rd show with Hauser and Wirth; Jon Rafman appears as the definitive voice for high/low-brow production of AI video work.

I personally came of age during the golden era of this movement, and the artists involved have been massive influences on my work and the work of my peers. To be very clear, I love Post-Internet art, and I am thrilled these people are all finally getting their much deserved shine. However, reading through the recent conversation on “Post-AI” art started by Avery Singer, I was struck by the feeling that it seemed to be the same heads dealing with things in a similar way, although with different input parameters. Where Post-Net 1.0 was defined by artists starting to grapple with the collapse of the divide between digital and physical into a causal and aesthetic unity, this renewed wave is more of the same classic critical twist in a new environment of realized Yarvin-style network control and platform ubiquity. New interrogations of identity and defense contracting juxtaposed with the possibility of infinite content.

There is a nascent movement of young artists that are dealing with reality and making work in a fundamentally different way: if Post-Internet art is art after the dissolution of the internet into the world, Hypermaterialist art is art that reckons with the ubiquity of intelligence in the material of the world itself, and how this self-consciousness dissolves into its own causal framework. When I refer to intelligence, I am not talking primarily about AI, or really about AI much at all. Instead I am thinking of artists who are interested in networks/non-human entities that have their own capacity for intention and spirit. More specifically, I am interested in categorizing the artists whose practices take this consciousness of reality as baked into the materials of their work.

In what follows I’ll try to briefly characterize the analytical framework for what Post-Net has gelled into as it has matured, will talk a bit about the aesthetic dialectics of the moment as I see them in a Kraussian style grid, and will try to situate a new movement that I have been calling Hypermaterialism against that backdrop.

After the Internet

It will be useful to give a quick rundown of what we mean when we talk about Post-Internet art. Obviously, these artists are not working within a monolithic framework, but what is given here is the broad strokes.

Post-Internet art is art made after the propagation of the internet. The internet, for a time, existed with power relations and causality that operated at different modes of complexity and non-linearity to the causal phenomena of pre-networked life. If modernism was arboreal, networks, specifically the widespread unoptimized networks of the late aughts, allowed for symbiogenesis. Post-Internet art sought to critique, use for content, and exploit those nonlinear relations as they became enmeshed with the phenomena of the rest of the world.

There were some aesthetic criteria for what constituted Post-Net. If the gallery PDF or instagram post was the object that drove commerce, interest, and validity in the world of fine art, why not embrace those domains and the aesthetics of digital spaces as primary material? Artie Vierkant (progenerator of the “image-object”), Petra Cortright, Pieter Schulwerth, Tabor Robak, Avery Singer, and countless others are examples in this domain. The side trend that accompanied and informed a lot of these aesthetics was the recycled early-internet pixelated GIFs, 3D matcap renders, and the digital holographics of vaporwave. Something that after the fact has been termed Fruitiger Aero, but a more fucked up version. My particular introduction to this aesthetic form was a Tumblr called lickycat run by someone named Bailey. There were thousands of Baileys. Photoshop and painting reached singularity. The author became dissolved or blurred unless the work needed to exist in a market. There was a lot of aesthetic overlap with memes.

The flex into branding was another popular move of the time. Just as institutional critique before it was a straight shot into the institution itself, work that engaged the platforms was potent on the platforms. The embrace of self-reflexive corporate aesthetics and “personal brand” are present in much of Post-Net but DIS, Amalia Ulman’s Excellences & Perfections, K-hole, Aids 3D, UV Production House are all examples of this thread within the conversation. Artists turned the mechanism of platforms and media back on themselves to interrogate ideas of increasingly atomized labor conditions. Ryan Trecartin invents the front facing camera. Social practice is just being Molly Soda.

Finally there was the absurd, disgusting, and beautiful “manmade horrors beyond our comprehension”. John Rafman’s sculptural work, weird images of food where it wasn’t supposed to be on the Jogging, Simon Denny’s Remainder series, Sean Raspet’s - 2012. I don’t think anyone made a work that was a compilation of ISIS beheadings with the snapchat cute dog filter, but they could have, and I might have cried.

All of these modes of aesthetics, of what the work actually looked like and did, had degrees of overlap. The potent and lasting conceptual framework that these aesthetics fell within is the collapse of media, life, and being into hyperstitional collage. The work collectively articulated the core of Post-Net’s ideological approach, conveying the alienation of a new modality of being as something glossy and disgusting and complicated. It was often post-studio, often produced in China, with low barriers to engagement. Looking back, it existed mostly as conversations between people trying to understand the self’s relation to a big mechanism that changed the basis of the economy, social life, and individuality. Post-Net saw the phenomena and complexity of the moment as emergent from the networks that were organizing everyday life; that networks revealed new properties of capital and social relations.

The approach often invoked blatant ironic distance, criticality, or collapse of sincerity into complexity. Every Post-Net artist worth their salt pissed someone off at some point because they were either making fun of something people liked or were perceived to be. A lot of the work was intentionally alienating, and while this is not a bad thing in itself, critically, the meat that made up the complexity of what these artists were trying to talk about sometimes outweighed the importance of the objects produced.

It is no coincidence that so many people involved in the movement have moved on to more didactic forms of media such as podcasting, video essays, and writing as primary modes of expression. Artie Vietkant just coauthored a book for Verso about Healthcare, Josh Citarella interviewed Fukayama, DIS is working as a consultancy, Rafman is a creative director, Seth Price is mostly known for his manuscripts, and Troemel is educating normies about economics and cultural theory. These artists in a real sense became what they were always destined to be. The self-reflexivity they used in thinking about the new ways of being in networks got integrated into the networks themselves. DIS totally redefined advertising, so the role of that self reflexivity collapsed into the function itself. Amalia Ulman made a narrative of herself in images so she became an autobiographical film maker. Simon Denny showed Metaverse paintings with Andreessen Horowitz at SXSW. Dan Keller became a stocks guy and seems to be doing well with it. Reality along with the capital forms of distribution and connection with which these artists were dealing were integrated back into the platforms themselves. The critique was metabolized in a way that had little effect on the superstructure it existed within. I will never forget hearing Kiernan Shipka claim in an interview that she was an anonymous meme admin.

Sculpture in the Expanded Field: Reloaded

In order to try and explain where aesthetics seem to be at the moment, I am going to attempt the hubristic task of constructing a grid like the one Rosalind Krauss puts forward in her seminal essay, Sculpture in the Expanded Field. I’ll start by explaining the two axes as I see them and then we will discuss what each of the quadrants entail and how they might exist aesthetically. These two axes have more to do with conditions of being at the moment than just the current modes of art being made, but there are parallels.

Emergence and Materialism

In a philosophical context, the idea of emergentism comes from an attempt to explain the “hard problem of consciousness” in philosophy of mind. The hard problem calls into question the idea that purely physical processes in the brain give rise to subjective, conscious experiences, or qualia. For example, let’s assume when I am subjected to a pain stimulus, “c-fibers” fire neuronal impulses up my spine into my brain resulting in me having the phenomenological experience “pain”. The mechanistic causal chain is definitely related to the conscious experience of pain, but it cannot explain the character of experience. The hard problem of consciousness asks: how could the unthinking processes of my body be metaphysically identical to the qualitative experience of pain?

Philosophers have taken different positions on this problem or ones similar to it through time, but essentially the answers fall into a couple camps. Dualism posits an entirely different substance, the soul, which is governed by different substantial relations than physical stuff. It is a relatively unpopular position for reasons I will not go into here. Reductive Physicalism, which emergentism falls within, is the assertion that subjective phenomena, or mental stuff, is in the end reducible to physical stuff. Panpsychism is the assertion that all stuff has mental properties, that consciousness is a persistent and fundamental feature of all of reality.

Historically, and I know this is sometimes surprising to a contemporary audience, panpsychist materialism was basically consensus within the philosophical community until the popularity of Logical Positivism came in the mid 20th century. Logical positivism claims that all things that are True are either true a priori, or are empirically verifiable. It attempts to end the question of metaphysics all together along strictly empirical lines. The movement was one of rigid analyticity, which socially coincided with the developing modernity of an industrial west. It is no mistake that the era of grand mechanistic narratives of the state and the moral imperatives of those bodies is one of arboreal and metallic relations to the mind and spirit. This is not intended as ethical argumentation for or against the positions, it is just to give some context on the cultural background of the school of thought.

Because the hard problem of consciousness is a real problem for the physicalist, a slew of explanations came about to make sense of mental events as rooted in a physical framework. Emergentism is the idea that physical stuff has properties which cannot be understood in the micro scale, but when observed at specific scales or configurations, begin to exhibit wholly novel properties. A good example of emergence is dots on a printing matrix of an image. There is nothing intrinsic to a dot of ink that enables it to represent Marilyn Monroe in a Warhol, but when organized appropriately, those dots of ink have the emergent property of representing Marilyn Monroe. Emergentism holds that consciousness is a property like this, which emerges from the mechanism of the body through the aggregation or abstraction of mechanical processes.

In contrast to emergence, panpsychist materialism bites the bullet on phenomenal experience and claims that at some level, all things have a form of phenomenal experience because consciousness is a fundamental property of all material. Phenomena and extension are two sides of the same coin. There is a “what it is like”-ness to all things.

There are different approaches, but it would not be off base to say that the panpsychist materialist would claim that electrons, societies, kidneys, people, and the universe all have their own form of experience. The Leibnizian view, which I am inexplicably fond of, holds that “my liver cells”, “my liver as a whole”, “my liver and the internet”, and “me including my liver and the internet” are all distinct minds with intention which literally inform reality through their interstitial relationships. It’s a weird position. More colloquial forms of panpsychist materialism might be your aunt talking about the intentionality of the universe.

To speak briefly about what is at stake between the materialist panpsychist approach and emergentism, emergentism gives us a basic explanation of why we have phenomenal experiences. It does not give us intentionality or a sort of governing set of psychic laws which would determine how phenomenal experience as a global property might have the causal force we might want it to. Both ways of understanding the properties of reality work across scales. The emergentist might say societal causation happens because certain scopes of the abstraction of certain types of matter have certain emergent properties. The panpsychist materialist might say a society has a mind of its own which exercises a top down effect on the matter it is composed of, while the matter it is made of fights back or coheres with its own intentionality.

For the sake of simplicity, I am going to refer to panpsychist materialism simply as materialism which I think will make more sense once we discuss the art that winds up fitting into each of these camps.

Absolute and Reflexive

While these concepts require less explication than emergence and materialism, they are worth describing for a minute. Reflexivity is to look at the state or narrative of reality as a plastic, but real, clear, and distinct thing. Reflexive approaches refer back to the thing itself in a feedback loop, where the mode of processing has an influence on reality. Its essence changes or clarifies when observed or interrogated. It relies on reality being in a constant state of becoming.

Absolute approaches take history, morality, beauty, and value to be things that have real and unchanging designations of properties. The absolute approach does not intrinsically assert that we know what those real referents of things like beauty and value are, but asserts that they may be discovered through a process of refinement where the goal posts stay roughly static.

The reflexive approach engages in a soft form of objectivity which is based around intersubjectivity in the constant clarification of the good, meaningful, or true, the absolute approach attempts to assert the state of universal properties and drive towards them. Reflexive approaches posit real, or causally effective, properties that instantiate in their discovery rather than the other way around.

Absolute Emergence: Neo-Modernism

I am not going to spend much time talking about the revival of modernist approaches. If you are reading this article, chances are you have seen the absolute glut of post-figurative painting and geometric abstraction which has been flooding the market. This work is a lot of what I mean when I talk about Neo-Modernism. The continued interest in identity based work and formalist art fits in this category. There is heavy focus on individual exceptionalism, the artists aren’t really asserting anything, and it mostly acts in the domain of process and therapy. Modernism in a real sense was the advent of subjectivity in our exploration of value. This new wave asserts that not only is value subjective, it is absolutely subjective; that there is nothing there beneath the skin; that social construction is all there is, but it does not point to some property and it’s not causal. It is an axiological nihilism of sorts with respect to what art is capable of. The Neo-Modernist approach to value is that the emergent property of what makes a work good is that it’s called good, subjectivity, market effects, and all. It is the anesthetist of critique and conceptual redefinition as a power of aesthetic meaning. Read a review of any of this stuff and you would be hard pressed to find a single thing that the work is doing other than being a singular art object.

This all sounds extremely negative, but to be totally honest, I actually really like a lot of this work. It's often fun, pretty often well executed, it feels personal to look at. If it does have some end to it, it just makes me love the world I experience everyday more, probably because I exist in a similar subjectivity and milieu as a lot of the people making it. Joe Speier, Shelley Uckotter, and Abby Lloyd are three of my favorite artists and they fit firmly into this category. There is some goofy deflationary conceptualism like Darren Bader’s show that was just up at Matthew Brown that fits in as well. Any sculptor that talks about liminal space fits in here. Experimental abstract photography, abject beauty, new art that looks like shit that would make sense at Dia Beacon, put it straight into my veins.

There are a lot of examples of this done poorly as well. If you have seen a show at a vanity gallery in Chelsea, 9 times out of 10 it fits squarely into this category of an artist doing things a little bit differently but often winding up with a painting that makes sense in the tradition of a lot of other paintings from modernism, but less well executed, and maybe just not that interesting to look at.

Absolute Materialism: Return

If you are reading this article you are also no doubt familiar with the “return to tradition” that seems to be rampant in culture, maybe more so than in art. I think this stuff has always sort of existed, but the thrust of the conceptual approach is: there is a distinct telos to value, and that telos is materializing the will of God by reflecting immanence. I think in this category, there are those that definitely believe they understand what it would mean to reflect the will of the divine in objects, and others who just strive to get closer to something out of reach. This work is often grand in scale and relies on extreme levels of labor and technical skill to actualize. There are probably 50,000 people on earth now who can paint as well as Vermeer or sculpt like Michelangelo, and if I could too, maybe I would be satisfied for that to be the end of aesthetics.

The bad versions of this work are things like Daniel Arsham, the African Mahogany KAWS at the Brooklyn Museum, or hyperrealist-baroque and renaissance revival. I feel like when I think of it, in my mind I can almost taste the hustle-preneur flavored instagram reel that accompanies its “grand creation” status. It's got all the gloss, it's EPIC, but it fails to transcend because I just don't buy it being all there is. The best version is work like Ivana Bašić’s which is ambitious, spiritual, and truly transcends without needing to complicate the purity of the aesthetics with criticality or concepts at all. Koons, even with all his PoMo tendencies – when you are staring at a 20 foot tall mirror polished bronze of a deer being hunted by a dog, hits in much the same way. I could care less about how lazy the paintings are. We all know why we are really there.

Functional “sacred small pleasures” or “fewer better things” style craft fits in here, maybe even the rash of realistic airbrush on canvas stuff we’ve seen pop back up in the past few years. I think there is a place here for burner art and stuff about crystals where the art is just a really big cool crystal. It all is trying to get to a glorification of the one true spirit of reality, either the subtlety or the whole of it, there are just a lot of different ideas of what that spirit is. It is often, by necessity, not that self aware. Most of the bad end of it reminds me of the song Comfort Eagle by Cake. The good end reminds me to never forget to truly believe.

Reflexive Emergence: Post-Net

Because I have already spoken at length about Post-Net, I’ll just discuss here how it fits into the grid and the critical limitations I see as bracketing the movement from other contemporary work. Also, I should just state that there is other work that fits into this quadrant, but because Post-Net is in the zeitgeist again, I’m going to use that as the example. There are also new artists making work in this category, I think of Maya Man as the most prevalent example. In terms of lesser known people, I really like Morry Kolman’s and Kayla Drzewicki’s work. School for Poetic Computation, Rhizome, Maya’s space Heart, all seem to foster the new gen of this approach and seem to be adding a fun posi-core spin to things.

Post-Net’s aesthetic innovation was using self-reflexivity to determine and hyperstition the aesthetics of the new face of power relations. Of course there were modes of art making that influenced the modes of production it engaged with in a broader sense before, but the aesthetics of Post-Net became the exact aesthetics of the networks it was looking to critique. It was the first truly successful self-reflexive movement in that it became fully hegemonic. Minimalism in its time was similar but it was guided by industry much more so than Post-Net which seemed to work more in lock step.

The aspect of Post-Net that is in some instances a feature and in some instances a bug is its approach to the properties and effects in the world it attempts to make work about. If we treat the properties of contemporary connectivity as fundamentally emergent, the only thing that can really be done with them is a form of intensification, future casting, or critique that is necessarily ineffective. In some ways Post-Net was genuinely clarifying. It often coherently linked new forms of connectivity with the underlying political power structures that they emerged from. But in the end a lot of it was like pointing out that two trains were about to collide where success of the art hinged on the moment of collision. Simon Denny’s show The Founders Paradox, was a great show, but the fact that Peter Thiel loved it is a massive part of the work’s own historicization and in no small part is what makes it exceptionally meaningful to look back on. Ryan Trecartin’s early use of the extreme self and panoptic self-surveillance are things that, while visionary, are now essentially not any more shocking or different than looking at any influencer with over a million followers. Part of the struggle with emergence as an analytical tact is that the work can be metabolized fully into the power structures it critiques because it is just an intensification rather than something that pushes into the new. Post-Net allows for the aesthetic/spiritual in its criticality but in my own experience it fails to reach for transcendence. It is about pushing in, deconstruction, and definition of the stuff already in the world, rather than pushing through.

Reflexive Materialism: Hypermaterialism

The fundamental conceptual assertion of Hypermaterialism is that by complicating aesthetic, material, and referential relations we can push through the mundanity and eternal return of reality; through aesthetics, we can generate something which possesses novel phenomenal experience and causality. It is the belief that art can actually transcend, and rather than act predictively, it can steer reality in non-linear ways; that when I see the eyes of God in the mud and pain of the moment, I can have an experience akin to seeing a new spectrum of color. Hypermaterialist art attempts to create aesthetic experience that integrates the intentionality of conscious materials as authors in the work.

I do not believe that art will swoop in and save us per se, merely that it is not just determined by history and is a component in the causal chains of the process of history. There is not necessarily an ethical dimension to a lot of this work, just an imperative of engaging in the process of history as an active participant. History works in a modality of competing narratives which act dialectically and eventually are transcended. Rather than there being a simple linear progression, there is a series of states of movement, almost like writhing, and stepwise functions between them.

To break down the conjecture more completely:

(1) There is a state of history which is composed of the internal contradictions between the dominant narratives of the time and the information of the world, dialectics.

(2) The information of the world is non-conceptual content.

(3) Through aesthetic or preconceptual processes, that information can be metabolized into phenomenal objects which clarify the dialectics of the moment. This information, as turned into aesthetics, is inherently alienating from the hegemonic narratives of the moment. In other words, the bracketing of the world through aesthetics creates new phenomena which complicate history, preconceptually.

(4) Abstract concepts and new aesthetic expressions are formed reflexively, in a feedback loop, to define the new aesthetic and non-conceptual material of reality. The bracketing of the world through conceptualization of aesthetics creates new narratives which complicate history, conceptually.

(5) Those concepts, integrated into the narratives of history, dissolve or make incoherent the contradictions of dominant narratives and generate new contradictions leading to a new dialectical moment.

(6) This happens within all intersubjectivities across scales and is the essence of history itself.

To extrapolate a bit, this means that the information of the moment, its aesthetic expressions, and its conceptual abstraction are all causal, intersubjective, and phenomenal. There are qualia to these dialectical moments and the materials of them.

Examples of this line of thinking in contemporary theory are bountiful. Bratton’s The Stack is probably the seminal text of contemporary panpsychist materialism that integrates the self-reflexivity of the world in its own determination. Cyclonopedia can be read as non-fiction. Latour’s Actor-Network Theory is essentially Leibniz revived for the modern constructivist approach. Harman’s Object Oriented Ontology, and specifically Morton’s expansion on the idea of Hyperobjects and “realist magic”, outlines in a very direct way what this nascent movement in art is concerned with. All of these theoretical approaches have their own flavor but they are unified in their understanding of self-reflexiveness of phenomenal states in the world and those phenomenal states’ pervasiveness.

So what does it mean for an artist to make work that is aligned with conscious materials and reflexive definition of the world? I believe this is actually a much more traditional way of making art than many of the other approaches already discussed. The work of medieval devotional object making and architecture were using the new narrative causal structures of the time to create things that influenced and acted reflexively with those narrative structures. The cult of saints, and the devotional objects that embodied it, is an obvious example. Saints were in a sense hyperobjects themselves, being the sum total of the ways they shaped society rather than just masses of flesh and bone. The same is true for moments within early modernism where aesthetics was acting in a symbiotic process with the determination of material reality surrounding industrialization and mass production.

Similarly, Hypermaterialist art aims to use the objects of contemporary reality, objects with complicated qualitative states and instantiations, to make work reflexively with those complicated structures. It aims to make things that metabolize into new narratives of history rather than just intensifications of what already exists. Finally, it aims to act squarely in the domain of aesthetic experience. It is a raising of the complicated hypermaterials, that reality is now undeniably composed of, into the spiritual and causal domain.

Most Hypermaterialist art is in the domain of sculpture and “new media”. Materials lists are often complicated and long. Many are working in process based approaches where the movement through the network of production is much of the content of the work itself. Filip Kostic’s term “content collapse” is an extremely useful term for understanding this nascent movement and the non-physical nature of the materials much of this work is made with. Thanos in Fortnite at the MLK Memorial virtual museum is a hypermaterial. Thinking of some of these things as physically instantiated (the internet is a series of tubes and server racks) is sometimes useful. But dealing with them as materials through the primary media of qualia is a common tact that Hypermaterialist art takes. In other words, pieces of content, the outputs of networks, phenomenal abstractions, and their nonlinear instantiation is literally what many of these works are made of.

Complicity with Conscious Materials

Much of the impetus for writing this text comes from my own desire to place the work I am making in the context I see it and my peers generating together. I think of the work I’ve made so far, the piece Infinite Pain from this past year which simulated a C.Elegans connectome experiencing constant pain stimulus is probably the best example from my own practice in this domain.

To speak of some other examples, Filip Kostic’s Fortnite 007 Merciful Angel constructs a counterfactual narrative of personal and geopolitical history of the NATO campaign in Serbia in the 90s within a bootleg of Fortnite. IP expropriation and political circumstance until something new and spiritually meaningful flows out of it. Isabelle Frances McGuire's works using game material, low pop, and robots fit perfectly alongside it.

Andre Magana’s works recreating industrial mold tooling show a reflexivity of information and the wealth of generation that is available in the data of the world. His Blackspot series of expropriated complaint images of Samsung commercial display units deal with climate, technology and bureaucracy in ways that are both a whistle blow and abstract image making. Ellis and Parker Von Sternberg’s New Works show at Kings Leap uses crime scene photos of concealed corpses and a convoluted frame shop order process as materials. Legal contracts make up half of the work. The glitter shrinkwrapped human remains in the basement of the space invoke a very “is it real?” feeling until you are left realizing “it's all real”, and it doesn't really matter either way.

Karyn Nakamura’s AI and optical tweezer stop-motion installation Surface Tension shows the drama of imaging and its extensibility, literally turning dead neurons into hands that reach across the network for connection. It’s loud and weird aesthetically, I have no idea what it makes me feel but it’s beautiful. Brian Oakes’ physically instantiated random number generator that was the centerpiece of their exhibition Seed last year stands to make concrete the random generation that enables all networks and computers to be able to run. I have it on good authority that they’re trying to make opals in their kitchen and just figured out how to print their name in rubies. Colleen Hargaden’s Anthropogenic Mineral Collection publication uses quantification and categorization as a way of giving mass to the interconnectedness and effectiveness at a geologic level to crystal formation.

Greg Carideo’s work, generating miniature scale hybrids between awnings and cathedrals from the detritus of rotting found steel, cotton, and shoe heels. It reminds me more than any work I’ve seen of the Jordan Peterson quote “there are cathedrals everywhere for those with eyes to see” while gazing over a refracting Evian bottle. The specificity is so important in the work but it also feels unknowably dense, like the same specificity exists in everything. Harry Gould Harvey IV uses a similar divinity in the work, using specific detritus from rapidly deindustrialized Fall River factories to create the literal framing devices for work that looks in between Quaker friendship drawings and kabbalah. Clare Koury turned a room into a microphone to listen to the Schulman Resonance of earth, the work also seemed, to some extent, to be about the copper market and copper as an alchemical material. In a similar vein Rachel Rosheger is dealing with copper, the history of its production and alchemical power in ways that link HVAC systems and perpetual motion. These four, more than most others in this group, exemplify the ‘realist magic’ which Hypermaterialism hopes to embody.

I don’t know who to group Mark Fingerhut with exactly because the work is so goddamn innovative. Spiritual computer viruses that turn your machine into a conversation partner that he uses to pour his heart out about relationships, pain, love, and the contemporary condition of alienation, Jesus Christ. If you have a Windows computer and you have not run Goblin.exe I literally can’t think of a better art experience to spend 15 minutes with. Though on a totally different part of the spectrum, the hyper-collage of Crisis Acting, an anonymous video artist, is one of the more affirming and expansive artistic presences I can think of. I am particularly taken by their video rendition of The Waters Of March which is probably the prime example of content as material. Both works make me feel similarly.

Joseph Greer’s collage of natural-industrial parity feels like constructivist sacred geometry in a good way, like he’s actively courting making paintings in space for the Demiurge. Rachel Jackson and Brandon Bandy’s recent exhibition making hydrodipped, printed, mangled wood components in a woodpaneled basement seemed to engage in this form of material reflexivity. The exhibition they put on titled Network Spirituality after the Milady “I long for a Network Spirituality” motto pretty much sums up and puts a pin on the total of what I am trying to describe.

I could go on and on but the point is that there are dense threads to this idea that laid latent for a long time. Almost all of these artists are under 35, there are maybe only a handful of cases where any production of the actual work is outsourced (and even in those cases that is often the point), and they all engage in the hypermaterials that dictate the spiritual and conscious flow of our time.

Transcending the Edge

I want to finish this out with a few quick points. The first is very quick: I live in NYC and it is for that reason alone that this list is geographically centered on NYC. This is what I see happening around me, but I’m sure it is happening elsewhere in slightly different flavors and modalities. Write about the examples or counterexamples, I’d love to see them, send me a link when it’s published.

Second, I want to acknowledge that there are obviously edge cases to consider. So it is in the complicated forward march of history. There is a cluster of artists that were around during Post-Net but feel closer to Hypermaterialism in some ways. Agnieszka Kurant, Rachel Rossin, Anthony Discenza, Trevor Paglen, some of Simon Denny’s new work, there are more. These people feel on the edge of embracing information in a new way, but a lot of the aesthetics and conversations wind up gelling with Post-Net more so than the new movement. Some of them are more on the post-studio end of things, some not, they also have just been in the game longer, they all give seriously good artist talks. I’m not totally sure but it feels like a meaningful cluster to identify. I’m sure there are other edge cases in the diagram as well but they just aren’t as clear to me.

Finally, I want to say briefly what Hypermaterialism means to me, on an emotive or personal level. We are in a moment where the stagnant pain of neoliberalism and imperialism invades every moment of our being. When I look into the world, I constantly see infinite suffering reflected back through genocide, poverty, hunger, and inequality. In a linear sense, I have no idea what to do about it. I cannot stop the murder of children by saying stop or through protest or voting. I cannot solve the growing problems of addiction and despair from a broken healthcare and financial system. I cannot donate money I do not have to everyone destabilized, or make it so that the rent stops being due to corporate structures more powerful and emboldened than we have ever seen. It feels more difficult than ever to heal the pain of the world even in small ways.

But still, I wake up every morning, and all the complexity and tension of reality washes over me and in the mottle of their colors I see and experience beauty and God in them. In the tears, and in the acid rain that washes them away, is a new spectrum of color that blurs with me like we are films in a dance of crossfade. It is inexpressible as words. My goal, and if I can be so bold, the goal of Hypermaterialism, is not to make sense of the pain of the world or ameliorate it through linearity. It is not to tell the world to change from a distance and watch it follow commands. It is to help the world transcend by showing it the beauty within it until it becomes so saturated that it begins to show through the skin. That the world, the things of it, and I, all of us, can decide together to be different, to make something closer, until the suffering fades and changes into something different and horrifying and beautiful in new ways.
author: Do Not Research
